newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica deals casino permits, firms aim at jackpot.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica deals casino permits, firms aim at jackpot.

text.p: After years of official disapproval of gambling during apartheid, South Africa has given its formal go-ahead for new casino licences.

The northern province of Mpumalanga on Tuesday became the first South African region to name preferred bidders for three gambling complexes and industry figures said on Wednesday they were looking to apply for more.

Under the previous white-ruled government, puritanical laws forbade gaming houses. This forced entreprenuers like Sun City-founder Sol Kerzner to build their Las Vegas-style resorts in nominally independent black homelands that Pretoria failed to get the rest of the world to take seriously.

In Mpumalanga, Tsogo Sun, a joint-venture between a black consortium and South African Breweries hotels unit Southern Sun, has been selected for resorts in the cities of Witbank and Nelspruit, while Global Resorts has been chosen for Secunda.
Tsogo chief executive Jabu Mabuza told Reuters his group was keeping an eye out for other provinces to offer licences and try to tap into the potentially huge market.
"We see ourselves as a player that is going to apply for licences throughout the country," he said.
Mabuza said he thought it was likely that Gauteng -- South Africa's most populous region containing Johannesburg and Pretoria -- would be the next to tender for applications.
KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape would probably follow soon after, he added.

The only thing preventing Tsogo and Global Resorts from starting work on their gambling palaces is a routine probity investigation by the Mpumalanga Gaming Board, scheduled to finish by the end of March.

The South African industry looks like a prize worth seeking. Consultants Ernst & Young have valued existing casino spending in the country at four billion rand ($855 million) a year. Even in the years of apartheid South Africans flocked to the homelands and neighbouring countries to gamble.

Tsogo aims to build a 360 million rand resort at Witbank and a 320 million rand one at Nelspruit. The complexes will have hotels, restaurants and shops as well as the all-important casinos. Construction should take about a year.
Global Resorts plans a 200 million rand resort at Secunda.
The South African government is keen to get the industry started after long delays to a National Gambling Act were overcome last year.

The legislation standardises South African law after the black homelands were incorporated back into the newly democratic country following 1994 elections. There had been a hotch-potch of gambling laws and venues.
A successful industry will provide the government with much-needed tax revenues.

Mpumalanga, which still has one more licence to award, says it cannot calculate exactly the benefits the industry will bring to the provincal economy, but that they are likely to be large, including the creation of about 4,000 permanent jobs.
"The spin-offs are so wide that it is difficult to put any final figure on it," said Andre Wilsenach, the Gaming Board's chief executive.
